Chance on trial

Inferential Statistics · Hypothesis Testing

Batch 7 of Dr. Jaideep Ghosh's lecture decks. Inferential Statistics builds the probability toolkit: sample spaces, three ways to assign probabilities, the rules, random variables, the binomial, Poisson and normal distributions, and the central limit theorem. Hypothesis Testing then uses that toolkit to ask whether a result could be pure chance: nulls and alternatives, significance levels, Type I and II errors, one- and two-tailed tests, the four steps, and confidence intervals for a proportion. The course intro says every test question comes from the slides, so every slide is on this page.

The batch in one breath

1 · Inferential Statistics

Inferential statistics lets you guess, test ideas and draw conclusions about a population from a small random sample. Probability (0 to 1) quantifies uncertainty. You assign it by the classical (equally likely), frequentist (past data) or Bayesian (prior judgement) method, and it obeys simple rules (all points sum to 1; P(A) = 1 − P(complement)). A random variable has a distribution: discrete ones have a PMF, continuous ones a PDF. The two key discrete distributions are the binomial (x successes in n fixed trials, mean np) and the Poisson (x events in an interval, mean = variance = λ); the binomial becomes Poisson when n → ∞ and p → 0. The normal is the key continuous one, with the standard normal Z = (x − μ)/σ. The CLT says sample means tend to a normal distribution as n grows (n > 30), whatever the population. In practice you use dbinom, dpois, dnorm or their scipy.stats twins.

2 · Hypothesis Testing

Hypothesis testing asks whether chance is a plausible explanation of your result. Sachin tells shaken from stirred mango lassi 20 times out of 23; if he were guessing, the binomial chance of doing that well is 0.0002, so guessing is doubtful. That number is P(outcome | hypothesis), never P(hypothesis | outcome). The null H₀ says the effect is pure chance; the alternative H₁ is its opposite (≠, > or <). Fix α (usually 0.05 or 0.01) before the analysis and reject H₀ if the p-value is below it. Rejecting a true null is a Type I error (probability α when H₀ is true); failing to reject a false one is a Type II error (β), and power = 1 − β. Tests are one- or two-tailed. A non-significant result is inconclusive: never accept the null. A 95% confidence interval that excludes 0 matches significance at 0.05; for a proportion it is p̂ ± z*·SE, e.g. 0.70 ± 1.96 × 0.015 = (0.671, 0.729).

Deck in one breath

Probability measures uncertainty on a 0–1 scale; you get it by counting equally likely outcomes, from past data, or from judgement. Random variables carry distributions: the binomial counts successes in n trials, the Poisson counts events in an interval, and the normal bell curve covers continuous data. Because of the CLT, averages of large samples are approximately normal whatever the population looks like, which is what lets you infer about a population from a sample.

sl. 1–7

What inferential statistics is

Slides: Inferential Statistics (title) · This material does duty for the course prerequisites · What is Inferential Statistics? · Key Concepts · Some Common Tools · Uncertainty and Lack of Complete Knowledge · Examples

Slide 2 says only that "This material does duty for the course prerequisites": the deck stands in for the statistics background the course assumes. sl. 2

Inferential statistics is "a set of tools that lets you make guesses, test ideas, draw conclusions or inferences about a large group of people or things (a population) by studying a small, random group (a sample)". sl. 3

Key concepts sl. 4

  • Population: the entire big group you want to study.
  • Sample: the small piece of the group you actually test or ask.
  • Generalization: you apply what you found in the small group to the big group.

Some common tools sl. 5

  • Hypothesis testing: checking whether an idea or claim about a group is likely true or just random luck ("already learned").
  • Confidence intervals: a range of values that likely contains the actual number for the whole group ("already learned").
  • Regression analysis: how one thing affects or predicts another ("coming…").

People make decisions under uncertainty, for example: Will sales decrease if we increase the prices of our products? Will the new on-the-job training program increase productivity of employees? Will the new investment be profitable? "DSA will help you address these types of questions." sl. 6

Six probability statements from everyday work sl. 7

WhoStatementProbability

Doctora patient has a 50-50 chance of surviving major cardiac surgery0.50
Meteorologist40% chance of rain tomorrow0.40

Business manager33% chance that product sales in her company will rise next year0.33
sl. 8–12

Probability and sample spaces

Slides: Probability Characteristics · Likelihood of Occurrences · Random Experiments and their Sample Spaces · Sample Spaces: Examples · An Example from Finance

  • Probability quantifies the likelihood of an event occurring; it quantifies the degree of uncertainty. sl. 8
  • It lies between 0 and 1. Close to 0 means highly unlikely; close to 1 means highly likely. sl. 8
Probability00.51
Reads as sl. 9Unlikely eventJust as likely as unlikelyLikely event
  • Outcomes of statistical experiments are governed by probabilities. Even when you repeat an experiment many times in precisely the same way, each outcome may differ: these are random experiments. sl. 10
  • Doing an experiment generates outcomes. The sample space is the collection of all experimental outcomes; one particular outcome is a point in the sample space. sl. 10
Experiment sl. 11Outcomes
Coin tossingHead (H), Tail (T)
Die rolling1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Product inspectionDefective (D), Non-defective (N)
One-day cricketWin (W), Lose (L)
Customer visiting a storePurchase (P), No-purchase (N)
Calls received per minute in a call centerTechnical issue (T), Nontechnical issue (N)

An example from finance sl. 12

SBI Mutual Funds has invested in two IT stocks. Possible profit or loss outcomes (₹) over six months:

InfosysWipro
+16−11
+13+21
−70

"Which is a better investment option?" The slide leaves the question open; the point is that the answer needs the probability of each outcome.

outside slidesIf the three outcomes are equally likely, Infosys averages (16 + 13 − 7)/3 ≈ ₹7.33 and Wipro (−11 + 21 + 0)/3 ≈ ₹3.33, so Infosys has the higher expected gain and the narrower spread (range 23 vs 32). With other probabilities the answer can change.

sl. 13–16

How to assign probabilities

Slides: How to Assign Probabilities? · Classical Method · Frequentist Method · Frequentist Method Example

Method sl. 13You assign probabilities…
Classicalassuming equally likely outcomes
Frequentistbased on experiments or past (historical) data
Bayesian / subjectivebased on subjective judgment using prior information or knowledge

Note: "We'll use Bayesian methods in spam detection problems." sl. 13

Classical method sl. 14

If an experiment has n possible outcomes, assign each a probability of 1n. The events are equally likely.

  • Tossing a fair coin in a test match (B = batting, F = fielding): Ω = {B, F}; P(B) = ½, P(F) = ½.
  • Rolling an unbiased die: Ω = {1,2,3,4,5,6}; P(1) = P(2) = … = P(6) = 1/6.

"This is certainly true if the coin and the die are fair (that is, unbiased)." sl. 14

Frequentist method sl. 15

If an uncertain event can occur in N mutually exclusive and equally likely ways, and n of these have a particular outcome, then

sl. 15P = nN = # of probable outcomes# of possible outcomes

Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time; the occurrence of one precludes the others. Heads and tails are mutually exclusive. sl. 15

Example sl. 16: roll a die; P(even #)? Ω = {1,2,3,4,5,6}, Even = {2,4,6}, P(Even) = 3/6 = 1/2.

outside slidesThe formula on sl. 15–16 counts equally likely ways, which textbooks usually file under the classical method; the frequentist idea proper is the long-run relative frequency, which the deck states on sl. 23 ("how often you get different outcomes when you repeat the experiment many, many times"). If a test asks, use the slide labels.

sl. 17–22

Events and probability rules

Slides: Events and Probabilities · Probability of an Event: Example · Probability Rules · Mutually Exclusive Events · Independent Events · Points to Remember

An event is one or more (a whole collection of) sample points. Its probability equals the sum of the probabilities of all the sample points that make it up. sl. 17

  1. Identify all the sample points corresponding to the event.
  2. Calculate or assess the probability of each point.
  3. Compute the probability of the event.

Example sl. 18: toss two identical coins (Coin A, Coin B) simultaneously but independently. Ω = {HH, HT, TH, TT} ("collection of all events"). P(H and T) = 2/4 = 1/2, because both HT and TH give one head and one tail.

Rules sl. 19

  • The probabilities of all sample-space points sum to 1.
  • P(event) = 1 − P(complement event). The complement of A is every sample point not in A.
  • Example: Ω = {H, T}; P(H) + P(T) = 1 ("one of these must happen"); P(T) = 1 − P(Tc) = 1 − P(H) = ½; P(T) + P(Tc) = 1, and P(H) + P(Hc) = 1.

Mutually exclusive sl. 20

A and B are mutually exclusive if, when one occurs, the other cannot: they have no common sample points. The slide draws A and B as two separate circles inside the sample space Ω.

Independent sl. 21

A and B are independent if the probability of A is unaffected by the occurrence of B. Two tosses of the same coin are independent if one toss does not influence the other, "certainly true if the coin is unbiased".

Ghosh's view · Points to remember

The idea of mutually exclusive events is very different from that of independent events. Two events that are not mutually exclusive may be independent, or they may not be. sl. 22

outside slidesA quick way to see the difference: two mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities can never be independent, because if one happens you know for certain the other did not.

sl. 23–30

Random variables and distributions

Slides: Random Variables · Probability Distributions · Discrete Probability Distribution · Continuous Probability Distribution · Exercise – Discrete or Continuous? · Probability Distribution Function · Discrete Probability Distribution and Mass Function · Continuous Probability Distribution and Density Function

  • A variable is a quantity of interest that can be observed or measured; it can take random values or be constant in the population. sl. 23
  • For a population of interest, a random variable has a distribution of the probability of occurrence of every one of its values; it takes a set of values with different probabilities. sl. 23
  • "In the frequentist view, probability is how often you get different outcomes when you repeat the experiment many, many times." Example: roll a die; 6 possible values, each with probability 1/6. sl. 23

The probability distribution lists the probabilities of the values of the random variable. Toss two identical coins simultaneously and independently and record the number of heads: sl. 24

x (heads)p(x)
01/4
12/4 = 1/2
21/4

Discrete sl. 25

A discrete random variable has a number of outcomes you can count: male/female, black/white, counts of heads. It may take a finite number of values or an infinite set such as 0, 1, 2, 3, … Its distribution is a discrete probability distribution.

Continuous sl. 26

A continuous random variable has an infinite number of continuous outcomes: "You cannot count them!" Weights of employees, stock prices. Its distribution is a continuous probability distribution.

Exercise: discrete or continuous? sl. 27

The slide leaves every answer as "???". Answers below are this page's, reasoned from sl. 25–26 and sl. 39. outside slides

VariableTypeWhy
Class size in a universityDiscretea count of students
Stock priceContinuoussl. 26 lists stock prices as continuous
Number of accidents in a busy crossing in one hourDiscretea count; sl. 39 makes it a Poisson variable
UG student having a petDiscreteyes/no, two countable outcomes
Daily temperature in Delhi NCRContinuousa measurement on a continuous scale

Probability distribution function sl. 28

A probability distribution function lists the possible values of a random variable x "together [sic → together with] their probabilities of occurrence p(x)". It satisfies two conditions:

  • 0 ≤ p(x) ≤ 1: probability is always +ve and lies between 0 and 1.
  • The area under a probability function curve is 1.

PDF sl. 30

For a continuous random variable it is the probability density function (PDF). The slide sketches a smooth curve p(x) falling away from the vertical axis.

outside slidesFor a PDF, probabilities are areas under the curve over an interval; the height at a single point is not itself a probability.

sl. 31–37

The binomial distribution

Slides: Two Important Discrete Distributions · Binomial Distribution · Binomial Random Variables · Binomial PMF · Binomial Mean and Variance · Binomial Distribution Example · Solution

There are two important discrete distributions: binomial and Poisson. sl. 31

Set-up sl. 32

  • A sequence of identical and independent trials.
  • Each trial has two possible outcomes: call one success, the other failure.
  • P(success) = p, fixed; P(failure) = 1 − p, also fixed.
  • You count the number of successes x in a total of n trials.

Binomial random variables sl. 33

  • Toss a coin 50 times: X = # of heads.
  • A printer produces 1% defective prints: X = # of defective prints in the next 15 printouts.
  • 10% of bits sent through a noisy digital channel are in error: X = # of bits in error in the next 5 bits.
  • Births in a hospital: X = # of female births in the next 20 births.
Binomial PMF · sl. 34p(x) = n!x!(n − x)! px(1 − p)n−x
  • p(x): probability of x successes in n trials; n: # of trials; p: probability of success in any trial (fixed).
  • n! is factorial n: n·(n−1)·(n−2)···3·2·1. For example 5! = 5·4·3·2·1 = 120. REMEMBER: 0! = 1.
npmean sl. 35
np(1−p)variance
√np(1−p)standard deviation

Worked example sl. 36–37

Roll a single, unbiased, six-sided die 5 times. What is the probability that a six comes up exactly 3 times? Here n = 5, X = # of sixes, p = 1/6.

sl. 37P(X = 3) = 5!3!(5 − 3)!(1/6)3(5/6)5−3 = 0.032

outside slidesStep by step: 5!/(3!·2!) = 10; (1/6)³ = 1/216; (5/6)² = 25/36; 10 × 25/7776 = 250/7776 ≈ 0.0322. In R: dbinom(3, 5, 1/6); in Python: stats.binom.pmf(3, 5, 1/6).

sl. 38–44

The Poisson distribution

Slides: Poisson Distribution · Poisson Random Variables · Poisson PMF · Poisson Mean and Variance · A Very Important Theorem · Poisson Distribution Example · Solution

Use it when you want the probability of a given number of successes but the number of trials cannot be enumerated: discrete events occurring in a continuous way (over time, space, etc.). sl. 38

Poisson random variables sl. 39

  • # of telephone calls received by a switchboard in a given interval of time
  • # of stars above a certain brightness in a particular area of the sky
  • # of automobile accidents in a busy intersection of a city in one hour
  • # of births per hour during a given day
  • # of particles emitted by a radioactive source in a given interval of time
Poisson PMF · sl. 40p(x) = e−λλxx!

p(x): probability of exactly x events in a given interval (time, space, etc.); λ: mean of the distribution. Given a mean rate λ in the interval, the Poisson gives the probability that exactly x events occur. sl. 40

λmean sl. 41
λvariance (same as the mean)
√λstandard deviation
Ghosh's view · A very important theorem · "REMEMBER this"

When the number of trials n is very, very large (n → ∞) and the probability of success p is very, very small (p → 0), the binominal [sic → binomial] distribution simply becomes the Poisson distribution. sl. 42

Worked example: phone calls sl. 43–44

A person receives on average one call per 30-minute interval, at random times. What is the probability that in any particular hour 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 calls arrive? X = # of calls per hour; the mean per hour is 2, so X is Poisson with λ = 2 (convert the rate to the interval asked about) and p(x) = e−22x/x!.

x callse−22x/x!p(x)
0e−220/0!0.135
1e−221/1!0.271
2e−222/2!0.271
3e−223/3!0.180
4e−224/4!0.090

The normal distribution

Slides: Continuous Distribution · Normal PDF · Normal Mean and Variance · Standard Normal Distribution · Standard Normal Curve · Large-n Approximations of Binomial and Poisson

The most important (and popular) continuous distribution is the normal or Gaussian distribution, also called the bell curve. REMEMBER: the distribution is mesokurtic. sl. 45

Normal PDF · sl. 46p(x) = 1σ√(2π) e−(x−μ)²/2σ²
  • The slide glosses p(x) as "probability of obtaining exactly x # of events in a given interval (time, space, etc.)" [sic: copied from the Poisson slide; for a PDF it is the density at x]. μ: mean of the distribution. sl. 46
  • The distribution is symmetric about x = μ.
  • A random variable following it is a normal variate or normal deviate; written X ~ N(μ, σ²).
  • Note: probabilities from the normal need calculus and numerical analysis; "R, Python, and even EXCEL have functions to do this packages" [sic].
μmean sl. 47
σ²variance
σstandard deviation = width of the curve
σ ↑large σ: broad curve; small σ: narrow curve

Standard normal sl. 48

The standard normal distribution is a normal with μ = 0 and σ = 1.

Standard normal PDFp(z) = 1√(2π) e−z²/2
Z-scoreZ = x − μσ  ~ N(0, 1)

Z is a standard normal variate with mean 0 and variance 1, "also called the Z-score". sl. 48

Large-n approximations sl. 50: both the binomial and the Poisson (discrete) can be approximated by the normal (continuous) when the number of trials n is large. "It is for this reason that the normal distribution is so common in the large-n limit."

sl. 51–53

The central limit theorem and final words

Slides: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) · Implications of the CLT · Final Words

The central limit theorem (CLT) "has important applications". sl. 51

  • Suppose Xi, i = 1, 2, …, n are n independent random variables, each with its own PDF pi(x) (these may all be different), mean μi and variance σi².
  • The random variable Z = ΣXi / n is the "mean" of the Xi.
Σμi/nmean of Z
Σσi²/n²variance of Z
→ Normalas n → ∞, Z tends to a normal with that mean and variance
Ghosh's view · Implications of the CLT
  • The CLT, "a key result for statistical inference", says the larger the sample size, the closer to normal the distribution of sample means becomes.
  • It lets us draw inferences about the population from sample data without any knowledge of the true population distribution.
  • It holds whether the population is normal or skewed, provided the sample is large (say n > 30). If the population is normal, "it's even better": the CLT holds even for n < 30.
  • To find the probability of the mean, use the CLT for the mean; for a sum, use the CLT for sums.

sl. 52

Final words sl. 53

"Now you've learned all the basics of probability and statistics needed in DSA projects." You do not have to compute any of the distributions manually; you use functions from R and Python libraries, "You'll learn very soon how to do this."

Hypothesis TestingCould your result be pure chance? Nulls, α, errors, tails, and confidence intervals

SourceGhosh, Jaideep. "Hypothesis Testing." Lecture deck, DOM207 Introduction to Data Science for Business Using R and Python, School of Management and Entrepreneurship, Shiv Nadar Institution of Eminence, Monsoon 2026. 40 slides.

Deck in one breath

Assume the boring explanation (H₀: it's chance), work out how likely your data would be if it were true (the p-value), and reject H₀ only if that probability falls below an α you fixed in advance. Rejection can be wrong (Type I, rate α under a true null); non-rejection proves nothing (Type II, β; power 1 − β). Never accept the null. A confidence interval gives the same verdict: if the 95% CI excludes 0, the effect is significant at 0.05, and its sign tells you the direction.

Problem → methodCan Sachin taste shaken vs stirred lassi? → binomial 1-tailed test (sl. 3–4, 22). Male vs female salary equality → test with H₁ ≠, > or < (sl. 8, 10). Borrowers backing regulation → CI for a proportion (sl. 38–40).
Decision rulep-value < α → reject H₀; otherwise the result is inconclusive (never "accept H₀").
DataNo file from Data Files/. Numbers: 20 of 23, p = 0.0002; p = 0.0031; n = 920, p̂ = 0.70.
Builds onDeck 1's binomial and normal (sl. 34, 48). Leads into the t-test decks (B08).

sl. 1–5

What hypothesis testing is: the lassi test

Slides: Hypothesis Testing (title) · What is hypothesis testing (HT)? · A scenario for HT · So, what should you conclude? · What does this probability really mean?

  • You hypothesize something from theory, common sense or expert/public opinion, then collect data to see whether it is supported. Two outcomes: it's supported or it's not supported. sl. 2
  • When you interpret a result, someone may ask whether it "could have occurred purely by chance". sl. 2
  • Hypothesis testing (HT) is a statistical procedure to find out if chance is a plausible explanation of your result or there is some underlying, real reason for it. sl. 2

The scenario sl. 3

Your friend Sachin Tendulkar1 runs a restaurant in Delhi and says a mango lassi should be shaken well but not stirred. Can Sachin himself tell a shaken lassi from a stirred one? You give him 23 drinks; for each you flip an unbiased coin to decide whether to stir or shake it, then ask him which it was. He is correct on 20 of the 23. Are you convinced he has some intrinsic ability?

Historical note: R. A. Fisher explained HT with a similar story "abut [sic → about] a lady who was tasting tea". Footnote 1: "Any resemblance with the celebrity cricketer is purely coincidental!!!" sl. 3

What to conclude sl. 4

  • You cannot say he can. He could have been incredibly lucky. But is it plausible he was lucky to this extent?
  • Find the probability that he got 20 or more correct out of 23. The distribution is binomial: two possible values, correct (1) or incorrect (0).
  • The probability comes out to 0.0002. He would have to be extremely lucky, or he really can tell.
  • "You cannot prove false the hypothesis that he was actually guessing, but you're very doubtful that he was actually guessing." So there is evidence Sachin can tell shaken from stirred.

outside slidesWhere 0.0002 comes from: with p = 0.5 per drink, P(X ≥ 20) = [C(23,20) + C(23,21) + C(23,22) + C(23,23)] / 2²³ = (1771 + 253 + 23 + 1) / 8,388,608 = 2048 / 8,388,608 ≈ 0.000244. R: 1 - pbinom(19, 23, 0.5). Try it in the lab.

Ghosh's view · What the probability means

0.0002 is the probability that Sachin would be correct on 20 or more of 23 if he were just guessing. It is the probability of an outcome, given your hypothesis. It is not the probability of the hypothesis, given the outcome.

If the probability of the outcome given the hypothesis is really small, you have some evidence that the hypothesis is false. But "you should not compute the probability that the hypothesis is false". sl. 5

sl. 6–8

Null and alternative hypotheses

Slides: Null hypothesis (H₀) · Alternative hypothesis (H₁) · Forms of AH

Null, H₀ sl. 6

A hypothesis that some effect is due to pure chance, denoted by the symbol H₀. Bear in mind that the null is typically the opposite of your hypothesis (what you're trying to prove or anticipate).

Example: H₀: Sachin is simply guessing; he has no capability to tell a shaken from a stirred mango lassi.

Alternative, H₁ or Ha sl. 7

If the null is rejected, an alternative "falls in place". The alternative is simply the opposite of the null.

Example: H₁: Sachin has an intrinsic capability to tell a shaken from a stirred mango lassi.

Three forms of the alternative sl. 8

For H₀: Male salary = Female salary, "There're are [sic → There are] three common forms of alternatives":

#H₁Test type outside slides
1Male salary ≠ Female salary2-tailed
2Male salary > Female salary1-tailed (right)
3Male salary < Female salary1-tailed (left)
sl. 9–12

Tests of significance

Slides: Tests of Significance · Statistical Significance · What does significance mean? · How to conduct significance tests

  • A small probability makes the null doubtful. But how small? "There is no right/wrong answer to this." sl. 9
  • Usually the null is considered false if p < 0.05; a more cautious analyst might require p < 0.01 or p < 0.001.
  • Saying the null is false = you have rejected the null.
  • The probability value below which the null is rejected is called α or the significance level (SL). sl. 9

Statistical significance sl. 10

  • When the null is rejected, the effect is called statistically significant. This signifies only that the null of no effect is rejected.
  • It does not imply that the effect is important or strong: you are simply confident the effect is not precisely zero, and it tells you nothing about how large or important the effect is.
Ghosh's view · Remember

Do not confuse statistical significance with practical significance. A small effect can be highly significant if the sample size is sufficiently large. sl. 10

Example sl. 10: testing male-female salary equality (H₀), suppose the probability is 0.0031. The effect of unequal salary is statistically significant and the null that salaries are equal is rejected.

What significance means sl. 11: "An effect is statistically significant means that the effect is real and not happening purely due to chance."

How to conduct significance tests sl. 12

  1. Specify an α before doing your data analysis.
  2. If the analysis gives a probability below α, reject the null; if not, do not reject it.
  3. If a result is significant, it is of no concern how significant it is. If it is not significant, it does not matter how close to significance it is.

Note: this way of working is "more useful [sic → more useful in] applications in which you need to make a yes/no decision". sl. 12

sl. 13–16

Type I errors, Type II errors and power

Slides: Type I errors · Type I error and α · Type II errors · Type II error and β

Type I error sl. 13–14

  • A Type I error: the test rejects a true null.
  • Two common strategies: reject if p < 0.05; or reject if p < 0.01 (more conservative).
  • The threshold is α or the SL.
  • The Type I error rate is affected by α: the lower the α, the lower the Type I error rate.
  • "It looks like α is the probability of a Type I error. This is incorrect." α is the probability of a Type I error given that the null is true. If the null is false, you cannot even make a Type I error.

Type II error sl. 15–16

  • A Type II error: failing to reject a false null.
  • "In the strictest sense, a Type II error is not an error!" A non-significant test just means the data don't give strong evidence the null is false.
  • Non-significance does not support the conclusion that the null is true; consider the test inconclusive.
  • It can only occur if the null is false. Its probability is β.
  • The probability of correctly rejecting a false null is 1 − β, the power of a test.
Ghosh's view · Remember

Think of the probability as an indicator of the strength of evidence against the null rather than simply a binary reject/don't-reject rule. Rejecting the null is not an all-or-nothing decision. sl. 13

Compare: with a Type I error you incorrectly conclude the null is false when it's true. sl. 15

Decision ↓ · Truth →H₀ trueH₀ false
Reject H₀Type I error (prob. α)Correct: power = 1 − β
Do not reject H₀Correct (prob. 1 − α)Type II error (prob. β)

The grid assembles sl. 13–16 into one view; "1 − α" in the bottom-left cell is outside slides.

sl. 17–24

One-tailed and two-tailed tests

Slides: 1-tailed tests · 2-tailed tests · 1-tailed vs 2-tailed tests · Example · Significant results · Example of 1-tailed test · Example of 2-tailed test · Example of 2-tailed test – cont.

1-tailed sl. 17

In the lassi test, the binomial probability of 20 or more correct out of 23 under guessing is 0.0002, calculated for the upper/right tail. A test that computes the probability in only one tail is a 1-tailed test.

2-tailed sl. 18

Ask instead: "What is the probability of getting a result as extreme or perhaps even more extreme than the one observed?" That needs both tails: a 2-tailed test.

Example: μ = 0.5 sl. 20

2-tailed1-tailed
Nullμ = 0.5μ ≤ 0.5
Reject whenthe sample mean deviates greatly from 0.5 on either sidethe sample mean is ">>> 0.5" (much greater)
Alternativeμ ≠ 0.5"μ ≫ 0.5" [read: μ > 0.5]

Significant results sl. 21

When a probability is below α the effect is significant and the null rejected. "However, you should treat all statistically significant effects in exactly the same way" [sic → should not treat]. Example: you should have less confidence that the null is false if p = 0.047 than if p = 0.002. "Thus, rejecting the null is not an all-or-none thing."

outside slidesThe example only makes sense with "not"; it matches sl. 13 ("not an all-or-nothing decision"). Sl. 12 says the opposite for yes/no decisions ("it is of no concern how significant it is"). The deck holds both: a strict yes/no rule for decisions, and p as strength of evidence for interpretation.

1-tailed example sl. 22

Sachin, 23 trials: is he better than chance? H₀: p ≤ 0.5, where p is the probability of being correct on any trial. If rejected, accept H₁: p > 0.5, meaning Sachin is better than chance.

2-tailed example sl. 23–24

Test employee performance by reaction to a stimulus, fast vs slow. H₀: μfast = μavg. If rejected, two alternatives: μfast > μavg or μfast < μavg. The direction of the sample means decides which is taken: if the fast-reacting sample mean is significantly less than the average-performance sample mean, the fast group's population mean is less than "the sample mean [→ population mean]" for the average group.

sl. 25–27

Reading a non-significant result

Slides: No effect vs small effect · Lesson learned · Interpretation

  • A high probability value shows the data give little or no evidence that the null is false, but it is no evidence that the null is true either. sl. 25
  • "It is often impossible to distinguish a no effect from a very small effect." sl. 25
Ghosh's view · Lesson learned

Do not accept the null when you cannot reject it. Doing so can result in a serious error. "A nonsignificant result frequently amplifies our confidence that the null is false." sl. 26

outside slidesThe last line reads oddly. The likely sense: a non-significant result with an effect in the expected direction still leaves room for the null to be false, so it should not raise your confidence that the null is true. Quote it as written if asked.

Interpretation sl. 27: say there is no real evidence Sachin can tell shaken from stirred, but also no evidence that he cannot. "It is almost impossible to prove a negative result."

A funny example. One fine morning you claim you were the king Vikramaditya in an earlier life. With no evidence you can hardly convince your friends, but your friends are also unable to prove for sure that you were not the king Vikramaditya in one of your earlier lives.

sl. 27
sl. 28–31

The four steps of hypothesis testing

Slides: Steps of HT – Step 1 · Step 2 · Step 3 · Step 4

  1. Specify the null. 2-tailed: typically that a parameter equals zero, μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 → μ₁ = μ₂. 1-tailed: that a parameter is ≥ 0, or that it is ≤ 0. sl. 28
  2. Specify α, the SL. Once fixed, you'll NEVER change the SL, no matter what. Typical values 0.05 and 0.01; 0.1 is sometimes used, "but try to avoid it". sl. 29
  3. Compute the probability, the p-val: the probability of obtaining a sample statistic as different or even more different from the parameter in the null, assuming that the null is true. sl. 30
  4. Compare with α. Smaller → reject the null; the smaller it is, the higher your confidence the null is false. Higher than α = 0.05 → findings inconclusive. Failure to reject does not support the null; it just means you lack data to reject it. Never accept the null. sl. 31
sl. 32–34

Confidence intervals

Slides: The Confident [sic → Confidence] Interval · 95% CI · CI and Significance Tests

  • A confidence interval is a range of values likely to contain the true value of an unknown population parameter. sl. 32
  • It comes with a confidence level, typically 95%: the probability that a repeated sampling method would produce intervals containing the true parameter.
  • Calculated as point estimate (e.g. a sample mean) ± margin of error.
Ghosh's view · CI and significance tests
  • If a statistic is significantly different from 0 at the 0.05 level, the 95% CI will not contain 0.
  • All values in the CI are plausible values for the parameter; values outside it are rejected as plausible.
  • IMPORTANT: when an effect is significant, all values in the CI lie on the same side of zero (all +ve or all −ve). So a significant finding lets you specify the directionality of the effect.

sl. 34

sl. 35–40

Proportions: theory and a worked CI

Slides: HT for Sample Proportions · Theory for Sample Proportions · In practice · Example · Solution · Solution Cont.

As with the sample mean, you can model a sample proportion p̂ with a normal distribution when the sample observations are independent and the sample size is sufficiently large. sl. 35

Theory sl. 36

The sampling distribution of p̂ from a sample of size n, drawn from a population with true proportion p, is approximately normal when:

  1. The observations are independent (e.g. a simple random sample).
  2. You see at least 10 successes and 10 failures: np ≥ 10 and n(1 − p) ≥ 10. This is the success-failure condition.
Standard error · sl. 36SE = √p(1 − p)n
mean of p̂ = p
CI for p · sl. 37p̂ ± z* · SE

In practice sl. 37

  • You hardly ever know the true p, so you substitute a value to check the conditions and estimate SE.
  • For CIs, use the sample proportion p̂ to check success-failure and compute SE.
  • For HT, use the null value (the proportion claimed in the null) in place of p.
  • A CI gives a range of plausible values for p; when p̂ can be modelled as normal, it takes the form p̂ ± z*·SE.

Worked example: loan borrowers sl. 38–40

A simple random sample of 920 loan borrowers was surveyed about regulation and costs; 70% supported new regulations on lenders. Can you model p̂ = 0.70 with a normal distribution? If so, find a 95% CI for p, the proportion who support increased regulation.

✓independent: it is a random sample sl. 39
644support: np̂ ≈ 920 × 0.70
276no support: n(1 − p̂) ≈ 920 × 0.30
0.015SE = √(0.70 × 0.30 / 920) sl. 40
1.96z* for a 95% CI
(0.671, 0.729)0.70 ± 1.96 × 0.015

Both 644 and 276 are at least 10, so the normal model is fine. "So, you're 95% confident that the true proportion of borrowers who supported the regulation was between 0.671 and 0.729." sl. 40

outside slidesUnrounded: SE = 0.01511, margin = 0.0296, CI = (0.6704, 0.7296). The slide rounds SE first, which gives (0.671, 0.729). The interval excludes 0.5, so a majority supports regulation at the 5% level.

Check the slide numbers yourself · every preset is a slide example

Quick revision

Both decks · surprise-test ready

The batch in ten lines

  1. Inferential statistics: learn about a population from a small random sample, then generalize (IS sl. 3–4).
  2. Probability ∈ [0, 1] quantifies uncertainty; assign it classically (equally likely, 1/n), by frequency (past data), or Bayesian (prior judgement; used for spam) (IS sl. 8, 13–15).
  3. P(event) = sum of its sample points; all points sum to 1; P(A) = 1 − P(Aᶜ). Mutually exclusive ≠ independent (IS sl. 17–22).
  4. Discrete variables have a PMF, continuous ones a PDF; 0 ≤ p(x) ≤ 1 and total area = 1 (IS sl. 25–30).
  5. Binomial: x successes in n fixed, independent trials; mean np, variance np(1−p). Poisson: x events per interval; mean = variance = λ. n → ∞, p → 0 turns binomial into Poisson (IS sl. 32–42).
  6. Normal N(μ, σ²) is symmetric and mesokurtic; Z = (x − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1). CLT: sample means → normal as n grows (n > 30), whatever the population (IS sl. 45–52).
  7. HT asks if chance explains the result. p-value = P(data this extreme | H₀), not P(H₀ | data) (HT sl. 2, 5, 30).
  8. H₀ = pure chance (opposite of your claim); H₁ = ≠, > or <. Fix α (0.05 / 0.01) first and never change it; reject if p < α (HT sl. 6–9, 29, 31).
  9. Type I = reject a true H₀ (α given H₀ true); Type II = keep a false H₀ (β); power = 1 − β. Non-significant = inconclusive: never accept H₀ (HT sl. 13–16, 25–31).
  10. CI = estimate ± margin; significant at 0.05 ⇔ 95% CI excludes 0. Proportion CI = p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1−p̂)/n) if np̂ and n(1−p̂) ≥ 10: 920 borrowers → (0.671, 0.729) (HT sl. 32–40).

Ghosh's verdicts

  • Mutually exclusive and independent are very different ideas (IS 22).
  • REMEMBER the binomial → Poisson theorem (IS 42) and that the normal is mesokurtic (IS 45).
  • You don't compute distributions by hand; use R and Python (IS 53).
  • Never compute "the probability that the hypothesis is false" (HT 5).
  • Significance ≠ importance; large samples make small effects significant (HT 10).
  • Rejecting the null is not all-or-nothing; p is strength of evidence (HT 13, 21).
  • Never change α once fixed; avoid 0.1 (HT 29).
  • Never accept the null; non-significance is inconclusive (HT 15, 26, 31).

Traps

  • α is not "the probability of a Type I error"; it is that probability given H₀ is true (HT 14).
  • The p-value is P(outcome | H₀), not P(H₀ | outcome) (HT 5).
  • A Type II error can only happen when H₀ is false; a Type I only when H₀ is true (HT 14, 16).
  • Poisson: variance = mean = λ; binomial variance np(1−p) is smaller than its mean.
  • Rescale λ to the interval asked: 1 call per 30 min → λ = 2 per hour (IS 44).
  • CI uses p̂ for SE; HT uses p₀ (HT 37).
  • Slide misprints to recognise: 98.4% [95.4%] (IS 49); "treat … in exactly the same way" [not] (HT 21); normal p(x) glossed as a Poisson count (IS 46).
  • Sl. 15–16 call the counting formula "frequentist"; textbooks call it classical.

Course lens

Problem → method

Price rise vs sales, training vs productivity, investment profit → probability under uncertainty (IS 6).

Which IT stock, Infosys or Wipro? → probabilities of outcomes (IS 12).

Calls per hour, accidents per hour → Poisson (IS 39, 43).

Defective prints, bit errors, female births → binomial (IS 33).

Can Sachin tell shaken from stirred? → binomial, 1-tailed HT (HT 3, 22).

Are male and female salaries equal? → HT with ≠ / > / < (HT 8, 10).

Fast vs average reaction performance → 2-tailed HT (HT 23).

Do borrowers back regulation? → CI for a proportion (HT 38).

Method card: hypothesis test

When: you must judge whether a result could be chance.

Set-up: H₀ (chance / equality / parameter = 0), H₁ (≠, >, <), α fixed in advance.

Compute: p-value under H₀ (binomial, normal…).

Decide: p < α → reject H₀, effect significant; else inconclusive.

Read: significance says "not zero", not "large"; check the CI's side of zero for direction.

Method card: proportion CI

When: estimating a population proportion from a sample.

Assumptions: independent observations; np̂ ≥ 10 and n(1 − p̂) ≥ 10.

Formula: p̂ ± z*·√(p̂(1−p̂)/n); z* = 1.96 at 95%.

Read: "95% confident the true proportion lies between …".

Code (IS 53)

dbinom() · dpois() · dnorm()
stats.binom.pmf() · stats.poisson.pmf() · stats.norm.pdf()

Self-test

Answer aloud, then reveal
—

Inferential Statistics

1Define population, sample and generalization.

Population: the entire group you want to study. Sample: the small piece you actually test or ask. Generalization: applying what you found in the sample to the population. (IS sl. 4)

2Name the three ways to assign probabilities, and where the deck says Bayesian methods will be used.

Classical (equally likely outcomes), frequentist (experiments or historical data), Bayesian/subjective (judgement from prior knowledge). Bayesian methods will be used for spam detection. (IS sl. 13)

3Two coins are tossed. What is P(one head and one tail), and why?

Ω = {HH, HT, TH, TT}; two of four points (HT, TH) qualify, so 2/4 = ½. An event's probability is the sum of its sample points' probabilities. (IS sl. 17–18)

4How do mutually exclusive and independent events differ?

Mutually exclusive: the events share no sample points, so one occurring rules out the other. Independent: the probability of A is unaffected by B occurring. The deck stresses these are "very different", and events that are not mutually exclusive may or may not be independent. (IS sl. 20–22)

5What two conditions must a probability distribution function satisfy?

0 ≤ p(x) ≤ 1, and the total area under the curve is 1. (IS sl. 28)

6PMF or PDF: which goes with which kind of variable?

PMF (probability mass function) for a discrete random variable; PDF (probability density function) for a continuous one. (IS sl. 29–30)

7List the conditions for a binomial experiment.

Identical, independent trials; two outcomes per trial (success/failure); fixed success probability p (so failure 1 − p is fixed); count x successes in n trials. (IS sl. 32)

8Give the binomial mean, variance and SD. What is 0!?

Mean np, variance np(1 − p), SD √np(1 − p). 0! = 1. (IS sl. 34–35)

9An unbiased die is rolled 5 times. P(exactly three sixes)?

5!/(3!2!) · (1/6)³ · (5/6)² = 10 × 25/7776 ≈ 0.032. (IS sl. 37)

10When is Poisson used instead of binomial, and what is special about its mean and variance?

When the number of trials cannot be enumerated: discrete events happening continuously in time or space. Mean = variance = λ; SD = √λ. (IS sl. 38, 41)

11State the "very important theorem".

As n → ∞ and p → 0, the binomial distribution becomes the Poisson distribution. (IS sl. 42)

12Calls arrive on average once per 30 minutes. What λ do you use for calls per hour, and what is P(0 calls in an hour)?

λ = 2 per hour; P(0) = e^−2 · 2⁰/0! = 0.135. P(1) = P(2) = 0.271. (IS sl. 44)

13Write the Z-score and state the mean and variance of the standard normal.

Z = (x − μ)/σ, with mean 0 and variance 1: Z ~ N(0, 1). (IS sl. 48)

14What does the CLT say, and what sample size does the deck give?

The distribution of sample means gets closer to normal as n grows, whether the population is normal or skewed, if n is large (say n > 30). If the population is normal, it holds even for n < 30. It lets you infer without knowing the population distribution. (IS sl. 51–52)

15Name the R and Python functions for the binomial, Poisson and normal.

R: dbinom(), dpois(), dnorm(). Python (scipy.stats): stats.binom.pmf(), stats.poisson.pmf(), stats.norm.pdf(). (IS sl. 53)

Hypothesis Testing

16What is hypothesis testing for, in one sentence?

To find out whether chance is a plausible explanation of your result or whether there is some underlying, real reason for it. (HT sl. 2)

17Sachin gets 20 of 23 right. Which distribution gives the probability, what is it, and what does it measure?

Binomial (correct/incorrect). P(20 or more correct | guessing) = 0.0002. It is the probability of the outcome given the hypothesis, not the probability of the hypothesis given the outcome. (HT sl. 4–5)

18State H₀ and H₁ for the lassi test.

H₀: Sachin is simply guessing, with no capability to tell shaken from stirred. H₁: he has an intrinsic capability to tell them apart. As a 1-tailed test: H₀: p ≤ 0.5, H₁: p > 0.5. (HT sl. 6–7, 22)

19Give the three forms of H₁ for H₀: male salary = female salary.

Male ≠ female; male > female; male < female. (HT sl. 8)

20What is α, and what values are typical?

The significance level: the probability value below which the null is rejected. Usually 0.05; more cautious 0.01 or 0.001; 0.1 is sometimes used but should be avoided. (HT sl. 9, 29)

21Does "statistically significant" mean "important"? Why not?

No. It means only that the null of no effect is rejected: the effect is not precisely zero. A small effect can be highly significant if the sample is large enough. (HT sl. 10)

22Define a Type I error. Why is "α is the probability of a Type I error" wrong?

Rejecting a true null. α is the probability of a Type I error given that the null is true; if the null is false you cannot make a Type I error at all. (HT sl. 13–14)

23Define a Type II error, β and power.

Type II: failing to reject a false null. β is its probability (only when H₀ is false). Power = 1 − β, the probability of correctly rejecting a false null. (HT sl. 15–16)

24Why is a Type II error "not an error" in the strictest sense?

A non-significant test only says the data don't give strong evidence against the null; it doesn't conclude the null is true. The right reading is "inconclusive". (HT sl. 15)

251-tailed vs 2-tailed: what differs? Give the nulls for μ = 0.5.

A 1-tailed test computes the probability in one tail; a 2-tailed test in both ("as extreme or more extreme"). 2-tailed H₀: μ = 0.5 (H₁: μ ≠ 0.5); 1-tailed H₀: μ ≤ 0.5 (H₁: μ > 0.5). (HT sl. 17–20)

26p = 0.047 and p = 0.002 are both below 0.05. Are they equally convincing?

No. You should have less confidence that the null is false at 0.047 than at 0.002; rejecting the null is not all-or-none. (HT sl. 21, 13)

27What is the Vikramaditya example meant to show?

It is almost impossible to prove a negative. Lack of evidence for a claim doesn't prove it false, just as a non-significant test doesn't prove the null: never accept the null. (HT sl. 25–27)

28List the four steps of HT, with the rule attached to step 2.

1 Specify the null. 2 Specify α; never change it once fixed. 3 Compute the p-value assuming the null is true. 4 Compare with α: smaller → reject; larger → inconclusive; never accept the null. (HT sl. 28–31)

29How are a 95% CI and a test at 0.05 linked?

If a statistic is significant at 0.05, the 95% CI excludes 0 and all its values lie on the same side of zero, which gives the effect's direction. (HT sl. 34)

30920 borrowers, 70% support regulation. Check the conditions and build the 95% CI.

Random sample → independent. np̂ = 644 and n(1 − p̂) = 276, both ≥ 10. SE = √(0.70 × 0.30/920) ≈ 0.015. CI = 0.70 ± 1.96 × 0.015 = (0.671, 0.729). (HT sl. 38–40)
